afghanistan: White with the Islamic declaration of faith in black script.
The tricolour it replaced in 2021 is still used at the United Nations.
Its country has had more than twenty flags since the early 20th century.
algeria: Green and white vertical halves with a red crescent and star.
Its design came from a liberation front during a war of independence against France.
Its crescent's horns are unusually long.
argentina: Light blue and white horizontal bands with a golden sun with a face.
Its sun has 32 rays, alternately straight and wavy.
First raised by a general on the banks of the Paraná River in 1812.
Its sun recalls a revolution in May 1810.
armenia: Red, blue and orange horizontal bands.
First adopted by a short-lived republic in 1918 and restored in 1990.
Its bottom band is sometimes said to be the colour of apricots.
australia: A blue ensign with a large seven-pointed star below the canton and a constellation of white stars in the fly.
Its large star once had six points, before territories were added.
Five people with almost identical entries shared first prize in its design competition.
Its neighbour across the sea has a similar flag with red stars.
austria: Red, white and red horizontal bands of equal height.
A legend links it to a blood-stained tunic at a siege in the Third Crusade.
Its colours are recorded on a ducal seal from 1230.
A Baltic flag looks similar but with a narrower white band.
azerbaijan: Light blue, red and green bands with a white crescent and eight-pointed star.
First adopted by the first parliamentary republic in the Muslim world, in 1918.
bangladesh: A red disc on dark green, set slightly toward the hoist.
Its disc once contained a yellow map of the country.
First raised at a university in 1971.
Its red is both a rising sun and the blood of a liberation war.
belgium: Black, yellow and red vertical bands, almost square.
Its colours come from a golden lion with red claws on a black shield.
First flown with horizontal stripes during an 1830 revolution.
A larger neighbour uses the same colours horizontally.
bhutan: A white dragon lies across a diagonal split of yellow and orange.
Its emblem clutches jewels in its claws.
One half represents royal authority and the other a Buddhist tradition.
The creature on it is also part of the country's name in its own language.
biafra: Red, black and green bands with a golden half-sun in the black band.
Its sun's eleven rays stood for eleven provinces.
The flag of a secessionist state in West Africa in 1967–1970.
A landlocked country in south-east Africa has a similar flag with a red sun.
bolivia: Red, yellow and green horizontal bands.
A seven-coloured square patchwork flag is co-official alongside it.
Its yellow represents mineral wealth in a landlocked Andean country.
brazil: A yellow diamond on green, with a starry blue globe crossed by a white motto band.
Its stars show a real night sky from the morning a monarchy fell.
Its motto comes from a French philosopher's school of thought.
Its green and yellow came from the dynasties of an emperor and his Austrian wife.
cambodia: A white temple on a red band between two blue bands.
The only national flag whose main emblem is a building.
Its temple appeared even on the flag of the Khmer Rouge.
canada: Red bars on either side of a white square containing a single red leaf.
Its leaf has eleven points, chosen after wind-tunnel testing.
A heraldic term for a central square as wide as the flag is tall is named after it.
It replaced a red ensign after a long parliamentary debate in 1964.
chile: White over red with a white star on a blue canton.
Often mixed up with a US state flag that has a vertical blue band.
Its white band stands for the snow of a mountain range.
First flown at its declaration of independence in 1818.
china: Red with one large yellow star and four smaller stars curving around it.
Its smaller stars each point toward the large one.
A hammer and sickle was removed from its design before adoption in 1949.
Designed by an economist who entered a national competition.
colombia: Yellow on the top half, then blue and red bands below.
Its colours were first flown by a revolutionary who reportedly discussed colour theory with Goethe.
Two neighbours, all once part of a union led by Bolívar, use the same colours.
Its blue band is said to represent two oceans.
cuba: Blue and white stripes with a red hoist triangle holding a white star.
A neighbouring island's flag has the same layout with reversed colours.
Designed in New York in 1849 for an expedition against Spanish rule.
Its three blue stripes stood for three military departments.
denmark: A white off-centre cross on a red field.
Legend says it fell from the sky during a battle in 1219.
Every other flag of its regional cross family is modelled on it.
Often called the oldest national flag still in continuous use.
east-germany: Black, red and gold bands with a hammer and compass in a wreath of grain.
Protesters in 1989 cut holes in its centre.
For its first ten years it was identical to its western neighbour's flag.
Its emblem stood for workers, intellectuals and farmers.
ecuador: Yellow (double width), blue and red bands with a condor-topped coat of arms.
Its arms show a snow-capped volcano and an early steamship.
Without its arms, it closely resembles a neighbour's flag.
Zodiac signs on it mark the months of an 1845 revolution.
egypt: Red, white and black horizontal bands with a golden eagle in the centre.
Its eagle is named after a 12th-century sultan.
Between 1958 and 1971 it showed two green stars from a short-lived union.
Its colours came from a revolution in 1952.
ethiopia: Green, yellow and red bands with a yellow star of lines on a blue disc.
Its colours became the Pan-African colours because the country was never colonised.
A lion holding a staff was removed from its centre after a 1974 revolution.
A religious movement in Jamaica reveres its former emperor and uses its colours.
finland: A blue Nordic cross on a white field.
A poet described its colours as lakes, sky and snow.
Adopted in 1918 after independence from an empire.
On its Flag Day, flags fly all night at midsummer.
france: A vertical tricolour with blue at the hoist and red at the fly.
The colours of its capital city were combined with the white of a royal dynasty during a revolution.
Its navy flies a version with unequal stripes so it looks even in the wind.
Decreed by a revolutionary assembly in 1794, it was banned for fifteen years after an emperor's fall.
georgia: A large red cross on white with four smaller red crosses in the quarters.
Adopted after a revolution named after a flower in 2003.
A version is shown on a 14th-century map at the city of Tbilisi.
Its large cross is that of the nation's patron saint.
german-empire: Black, white and red horizontal bands.
It combined the colours of a kingdom with those of a league of trading cities.
Chosen by a chancellor who rejected the colours of the 1848 revolution.
It was abandoned in 1918, briefly restored in 1933 and dropped again in 1935.
germany: Three horizontal bands: black on top, then red, then gold.
Its colours trace back to the uniforms of a volunteer corps that fought Napoleon.
A revolutionary parliament adopted it in 1848, but it became official only in 1919.
For forty years two neighbouring states used it, one with a hammer and compass added.
ghana: Red, gold and green horizontal bands with a black star in the middle.
Its star gives a national football team its nickname.
The first flag of an independent sub-Saharan African colony, from 1957.
For two years its middle band was white under a one-party state.
greece: Nine blue and white stripes with a white cross in a blue canton.
Its stripes are often linked to the syllables of a revolutionary motto.
For 150 years it was only the sea flag; a plain cross flag was used on land.
Its shade of blue has never been fixed by law.
iceland: A red cross edged in white on a blue field.
Its colours officially stand for mountains, ice and volcanic fire.
An earlier unofficial version was rejected partly for resembling a Mediterranean flag.
A nearby kingdom uses the same pattern with two colours swapped.
india: Saffron, white and green horizontal stripes with a navy wheel in the middle.
Its central wheel has 24 spokes and comes from an emperor's stone pillar.
A spinning wheel was replaced by a wheel of law weeks before independence.
Its flag code once required the flag to be made from hand-spun cloth.
indonesia: Red over white, two equal horizontal bands.
Almost identical to a European principality's flag, except for proportions.
Its colours are traced to a medieval Javanese empire.
Its first copy was sewn by the wife of the country's first president.
iran: Green, white and red with a red central emblem and stylised script along the band edges.
A religious phrase is repeated 22 times on it, for a date in its calendar.
A lion holding a sword under a rising sun was removed from it after a revolution.
Its central emblem is shaped like a tulip.
iraq: Red, white and black bands with green Arabic script in the centre.
Its script was once in a dictator's handwriting.
Three green stars were removed from it in 2008.
Its tricolour dates from a proposed union of three Arab states in 1963.
ireland: Green, white and orange vertical bands.
Its white band was described as a truce between two religious traditions.
Presented in 1848 after its presenter received it in Paris.
It flew over a post office during an uprising in 1916.
israel: A blue six-pointed star between two horizontal blue stripes on white.
Its design was modelled on a prayer shawl.
First used at a congress held in Basel in 1897.
italy: Green, white and red vertical bands with no emblem.
First adopted by a republic created in 1797 in the north of its peninsula.
A royal shield was removed from its white band after a 1946 referendum.
Its constitution defines it in a single sentence.
jamaica: A gold diagonal cross with green triangles top and bottom and black triangles at the sides.
The only national flag with no red, white or blue.
An earlier horizontal design was dropped for looking like an East African flag.
Its black triangles were once said to represent hardships.
japan: A single red circle centred on a white field, nothing else.
Its disc used to sit very slightly toward the hoist until a 1999 law centred it.
The disc evokes a goddess from whom an imperial dynasty claims descent.
jordan: Black, white and green bands with a red hoist triangle holding a white seven-pointed star.
Its star's points refer to the verses of a chapter of the Quran.
Based on the flag of a revolt against the Ottoman Empire in 1916.
A neighbouring flag is identical except for the star.
kazakhstan: A golden sun and eagle on sky blue, with an ornamental band at the hoist.
Its hoist band shows a 'ram's horn' pattern.
Adopted in 1992 after a competition, replacing a Soviet republic flag.
kenya: Black, red and green bands with thin white stripes, and a shield and two spears in the centre.
The shield on it is of a traditional pastoralist people's design.
Its colours come from the party that led the country to independence in 1963.
kuwait: Green, white and red bands with a black trapezoid at the hoist.
Its colours are described in a medieval line of poetry about deeds, battles, fields and swords.
It replaced a red flag bearing the country's name in 1961.
kyrgyzstan: A golden sun with 40 rays on red, holding the crown of a yurt.
Its rays stand for forty tribes united by an epic hero.
Its sun's rays were straightened in 2023 after being likened to a sunflower.
lebanon: A green tree on a white band between two red bands.
Its central tree touches both of the coloured bands.
Before independence its tree sat on a European tricolour.
libya: Red, black (twice as tall) and green bands with a white crescent and star.
Its predecessor was plain green, the only one-colour national flag.
A monarchy's flag revived by a 2011 uprising.
Its three colours stand for three historic regions.
malaysia: Red and white stripes with a blue canton holding a yellow crescent and a many-pointed star.
Its star and stripes kept a count of fourteen after one member left the federation.
Its yellow is the royal colour of its hereditary rulers.
mexico: Green, white and red vertical bands with an eagle eating a snake on a cactus.
Its emblem retells the founding legend of a city built on a lake.
Remove its emblem and it closely resembles a European flag.
Its current emblem was redrawn just before its capital hosted the Olympics.
mongolia: Red, blue and red vertical bands with a golden column of symbols at the hoist.
Its emblem was created by a 17th-century monk as part of an alphabet.
A communist star was removed from it in 1992.
Its central blue represents the 'eternal blue sky'.
morocco: A green interlaced star on a red field.
Its star was added in 1915 because plain red flags were confused at sea.
Its star is known by the name of a biblical king.
Its red is linked to a royal dynasty.
mozambique: A red hoist triangle with a star, a book, a hoe and a rifle.
The only national flag that shows an assault rifle.
Green, black and yellow bands edged in white, inherited from a liberation movement.
myanmar: Yellow, green and red bands with a large white star across them.
Introduced in 2010 under a military-drafted constitution.
Its predecessor had a cogwheel and rice plant in the canton.
Its colours echo a wartime flag that featured a peacock.
nepal: The only national flag that is not a rectangle.
Two stacked crimson pennants with a blue border.
A white moon above and a white sun below.
Its constitution gives step-by-step geometric instructions for drawing it.
netherlands: Red, white and blue horizontal stripes of equal height.
Its top stripe was originally orange, after a princely house.
On royal holidays an orange pennant is flown above it.
A neighbouring grand duchy has a nearly identical flag with a lighter blue.
new-zealand: A blue ensign with four red stars edged in white.
It survived a 2016 referendum against a silver-fern design.
Its neighbour's very similar flag has white stars and an extra seven-pointed star.
A flag chosen by Māori chiefs in 1834 preceded it.
nigeria: Green, white and green vertical bands.
Designed by a student in London; the judges removed a sun from the centre.
Raised at midnight at independence in 1960.
Its colonial predecessor showed a six-pointed star around a crown.
norway: A blue cross edged in white on red, offset toward the hoist.
Designed in 1821 by adding a blue cross to a neighbour's flag.
Its colours were chosen as colours of liberty, after three revolutionary-era nations.
A nearby island nation uses the same pattern with its colours swapped.
ottoman-empire: A white crescent and five-pointed star on red, from an empire that ended in 1922.
Its star was reduced from eight to five points during a reform era.
A republic kept its design almost unchanged.
pakistan: Dark green with a white crescent and star, and a white band at the hoist.
Its white band represents religious minorities.
Adopted three days before its country became independent.
Based on the flag of a political party founded in 1906.
paraguay: Red, white and blue horizontal bands with a different emblem on each side.
Its reverse shows a lion guarding a liberty cap.
Its front shows a star named after the month of its independence.
peru: Red, white and red vertical bands of equal width.
A legend says flamingos inspired its colours.
Its state version adds a shield with a vicuña and a cornucopia.
Its colours were chosen by a liberator from across the Andes in 1820.
philippines: Blue over red with a white hoist triangle holding a gold sun and three stars.
Flown with red on top in wartime.
Its sun's eight rays stand for provinces that rose against a colonial power.
Designed by a general in exile in Hong Kong.
poland: White over red, two horizontal bands.
Its colours come from a white eagle on a red shield.
Declared the national colours during an uprising in 1831.
Two other countries use the same colours upside down.
portugal: Green at the hoist, red in the fly, with a shield over a gold armillary sphere.
Its sphere was the emblem of a king of the Age of Discoveries.
Five small blue shields on it are linked to a legend of a 12th-century battle.
It replaced a blue and white royal flag after a revolution in 1910.
qatar: Maroon with a white hoist band and a zigzag edge of nine points.
The only national flag more than twice as wide as it is tall.
Its colour is said to come from red dye darkening in desert sun.
A nearby kingdom has a similar red flag with five points.
qing-dynasty: A blue dragon on yellow reaching for a red pearl.
The first national flag of a vast empire, created for naval and diplomatic use.
Replaced by a five-stripe flag after a revolution in 1911–1912.
russia: White, blue and red horizontal bands, with no emblem.
Traditionally linked to a tsar who studied shipbuilding abroad.
It disappeared for over seventy years and returned during a failed coup.
Its colours became the basis for a family of flags named after an ethnolinguistic group.
saudi-arabia: A green flag with white Arabic calligraphy above a horizontal sword.
It is never flown at half-mast because of the words on it.
It is made double-sided so its inscription reads correctly from both sides.
Its inscription is a declaration of religious faith.
singapore: Red over white with a white crescent and five stars in the upper hoist.
Its five stars stand for democracy, peace, progress, justice and equality.
Its crescent represents a young nation rising, not a religion.
Designed in 1959 for self-government, kept through a brief federation.
socialist-federal-republic-of-yugoslavia: Blue, white and red bands with a large red star edged in gold across them.
Partisans added its star during the Second World War.
Its federation broke apart in 1991–1992, leaving two republics to keep the plain tricolour.
Its six republics each had their own star-bearing flags.
south-africa: A green horizontal Y separates red and blue bands, with a black triangle at the hoist.
Six colours, no emblem, designed by a state herald in a matter of weeks.
First raised on the day of its country's first fully democratic election.
It replaced an orange-white-blue flag carrying three miniature flags.
south-korea: A red and blue yin-yang circle on white with four black trigrams.
Its corner symbols stand for heaven, earth, water and fire.
A diplomat flew it on a mission abroad in 1882, the year before it became official.
It was banned in its own country for 35 years of occupation.
south-vietnam: Yellow with three thin red horizontal stripes.
Its stripes stand for the three regions of a country it claimed in full.
It is still flown by communities abroad as a 'heritage and freedom' flag.
Its state ended with the fall of its capital in April 1975.
soviet-union: Red with a gold hammer and sickle under a star outlined in gold.
Lowered from the Kremlin for the last time on 25 December 1991.
Its reverse side was officially plain red.
Its tools stood for industrial workers and peasants.
spain: A yellow band twice as wide as the red bands above and below it, with a crowned shield toward the hoist.
Two pillars on it carry a motto meaning 'further beyond'.
Chosen by a king in 1785 to make his warships easier to identify at sea.
A republic in the 1930s replaced its lower band with purple.
sri-lanka: A gold lion with a sword on maroon, with green and saffron stripes beside it.
Its corner leaves come from the tree of the Buddha's enlightenment.
Its lion comes from the banner of a highland kingdom that fell in 1815.
Two stripes were added in 1951 to represent minorities.
sweden: A yellow Nordic cross on a blue field.
Its colours come from three golden crowns on a royal shield.
For six decades its canton held a mark nicknamed after a fish dish.
A legend claims a king saw its cross in the sky before a crusade.
switzerland: A white cross on a red square, not touching the edges.
One of only two square national flags.
Reverse its colours and you get a humanitarian emblem founded in its country.
Derived from the banner of one of three founding cantons.
syria: Green, white and black bands with three red stars across the white band.
Flown by an opposition movement for thirteen years before becoming national again.
First adopted under a French Mandate in 1932.
Its stars once stood for three districts, including Aleppo.
tajikistan: Red, a double-width white band, and green, with a gold crown under seven stars.
Its crown refers to a word for crown in its own national name.
Its capital once had the world's tallest flagpole.
thailand: Red, white, blue, white, red stripes with a double-height blue centre.
It replaced a flag with a white elephant.
A king is said to have designed it after seeing a flag hung upside down.
Its three colours stand for 'Nation, Religion, King'.
tunisia: A red crescent and star inside a white disc on a red field.
Introduced in 1831 after a fleet was destroyed at Navarino.
Used through a French protectorate and into independence.
turkey: A white crescent and star slightly toward the hoist on a red field.
Its star once had eight points, until a 19th-century reform era.
A legend links it to a moon reflected in pools of blood after a battle.
Its geometry was set by a law of 1936, inherited from an empire.
turkmenistan: Green with a red hoist band of carpet patterns, olive branches, and a white crescent with five stars.
Its band shows designs from five tribes' carpets.
Olive branches were added for its UN-recognised neutrality.
ukraine: Blue over yellow in two equal horizontal bands.
Popularly read as a clear sky above fields of wheat.
Its colours come from a golden lion on a medieval kingdom's arms.
Banned for decades and restored in 1992.
united-arab-emirates: A vertical red band at the hoist, with green, white and black horizontal bands.
Designed by a 19-year-old in a competition for a new federation in 1971.
Its seven member states each keep their own flags.
united-kingdom: Three national crosses, one upright and two diagonal, overlaid on a blue field.
It has a correct way up because its diagonal crosses are offset.
One constituent country is not represented on it at all.
It sits in the canton of several other national flags in Oceania.
united-states: Thirteen horizontal stripes of red and white and a blue canton full of white stars.
Its canton has been redesigned more than twenty times, a new version each time the federation grew.
A star is added on the Fourth of July after a new member joins.
A version with fifteen stripes inspired a national anthem written during a bombardment in 1814.
uruguay: Nine white and blue stripes with a golden sun with a face in the canton.
Its sun has sixteen rays, half as many as its neighbour's.
Its stripes stand for nine original departments.
It is one of three official national flags of its country.
uzbekistan: Light blue, white and green bands with red edging, a white crescent and twelve stars.
Its twelve stars stand for months and the zodiac.
Its blue was the colour of a 14th-century conqueror's banner.
venezuela: Yellow, blue and red bands with an arc of eight white stars.
An eighth star was added in 2006.
Its colours were first flown by Francisco de Miranda in 1806.
Its blue is said to be the sea separating it from Spain.
vietnam: A single large yellow star centred on red.
First used in an uprising against French colonial rule in 1940.
The flag of a former southern state, yellow with three red stripes, is still flown by communities abroad.
